source.title: Harmful Intent as a Geometrically Recoverable Feature of LLM Residual Streams

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures linear separability and geometry of harmful-intent decoding directions, and argues that these directions are protocol-specific rather than established computational features. It does not test sparse-feature superposition, capacity competition, SAE features, or the dimensionality of features that are superposed.
record.gate_note: The paper reports new results on residual-stream direction geometry, recorded below as findings that do not fit a claim version. It does not test the claim's proposed sparse-feature storage mechanism.
record.test_reason: The study probes harmful-intent directions in residual streams with supervised linear probes and measures their geometry across extraction protocols. It does not study sparse features exceeding dimensions, neuron polysemanticity, capacity competition, SAE dictionaries, or feature dimensionality. Its claim that probing finds a protocol-specific axis rather than the model's feature concerns probe identifiability, not superposition. SAEs appear only as suggested future work.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Authors conclude harmful intent is a stable linearly recoverable direction across architectures, alignment variants (including abliterated models) and scale. The direction is concentrated within a protocol but protocol-dependent across protocols, so probing does not isolate a unique computational feature. They also recommend reporting low-FPR metrics alongside AUROC.
record.recipe_differences: The study probes residual-stream activations and measures linear decoding and direction geometry; it does not use the Toy Models of Superposition setup or test sparse-feature storage.
record.method_sensitivity: Extraction protocol changes the recovered direction and the effect of projection: max-pooling versus last-token pooling, and raw versus chat-templated inputs. The paper also reports layer-dependent performance, particularly the Qwen2.5 projection-strategy valley.

fits_no_version.finding: Supervised linear probes decode harmful intent at AUROC ~0.98 across 12 small models. Directions are concentrated within an extraction protocol (refit after projection drops to 0.60 under mp/raw) but near-orthogonal across protocols (~73°). Projecting out the lt/chat direction leaves max-pool detection intact.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear-probe harm directions are protocol-specific decoding axes, not unique computational features of the model.

record.problems: The evaluation is single-turn, English, and uses cleanly formatted prompts; adversarial suffixes, multi-turn contexts, stylistically diverse harm, and cross-lingual prompts are untested. The authors state that their probing procedure recovers protocol-specific directions rather than the model's computational feature.
record.rows_left_out: Per-model projection/refit values in Appendices G, H, and I, per-model direction angles in Tables 2 and 9, and detailed classifier and detection-performance results were not included because they do not test any listed claim version; the aggregate geometric outcomes most relevant to the claim's subject are retained.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no sparsity sweep, no feature-count vs dimension geometry.
All: no neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity analysis.
All: polysemantic neurons are not examined.
All: no neuron-distribution measure and no dictionary/SAE recovery. A linearly decodable harm direction is not evidence about superposition.
All: no SAE features trained or evaluated.
All: the authors leave open whether the protocols see one feature or separate features, and do not test multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is right. All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The cannot_determine states are acceptable, since no row measures a version's effect. Detection-performance and cross-variant transfer results are reasonably omitted as irrelevant to the versions.

versions.untested_parts: Sparse features, feature counts exceeding dimensions, interference, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry in toy models.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure and what that implies about superposition.
Whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or sparse features are recovered by a dictionary or SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
Whether the features that are superposed are one-dimensional or multidimensional.

rows.subject: 12-model aggregate
rows.operation_detail: Measured the angle between the mp/raw mean-difference harm direction and the leading principal component of benign-prompt activations.
rows.note: Aggregate over the 12 main-set models; this compares a decoding direction with benign activation variance, not with a superposed feature.

rows.subject: 12-model aggregate
rows.operation_detail: Compared the mp/raw mean-difference direction with the mp/raw Soft-AUC-optimised direction.
rows.note: Aggregate over 12 models; the result concerns similarity between two fitted detection directions.

rows.subject: Four instruction-tuned models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Projected out the protocol's mean-difference direction from activations, then refit a Soft-AUC direction.
rows.note: The text describes a substantial drop from unprojected performance; the aggregate unprojected baseline is not stated.

rows.subject: Four instruction-tuned models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Projected out the protocol's mean-difference direction from activations, then refit a Soft-AUC direction.
rows.note: The paper says more detection signal remains than under mp/raw extraction; this is a result about protocol-specific decoding directions.

rows.subject: Four instruction-tuned models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Projected out the lt/chat mean-difference direction, then refit under mp/raw extraction.
rows.measure: Change in refitted effective AUROC; remaining mean-difference-vector norm
rows.value: AUROC change mean −0.002, at most 0.010 in absolute value; mean-difference vector retains ≥99% of its norm
rows.note: Aggregate result across four models. The paper characterises the change as within bootstrap noise.

rows.subject: Four instruction-tuned models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Projected out the lt/chat mean-difference direction, then refit under mp/chat extraction.
rows.measure: Change in refitted effective AUROC; remaining mean-difference-vector norm
rows.value: AUROC change mean +0.006, maximum +0.020; mean-difference vector retains 89–98% of its norm
rows.note: Aggregate result across four models. The paper characterises the AUROC change as within bootstrap noise.

rows.subject: Four instruction-tuned models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Projected out the lt/chat mean-difference direction, then refit under lt/chat extraction.
rows.measure: Change in refitted effective AUROC; remaining mean-difference-vector norm
rows.value: AUROC change mean −0.280, range −0.398 to −0.186; norm ratio below 10⁻²
rows.note: Aggregate result across four models; under this protocol the projected direction accounts for nearly all of the mean-difference vector.

rows.subject: Four instruction-tuned models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the angle between mp/chat Soft-AUC and lt/chat mean-difference directions.
rows.note: The directions retain high discrimination under cross-protocol scoring, but the paper does not identify either direction as the model's computational feature.
